screens.title: GPIO Fundamentals and Safe Circuit Design
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn what each Raspberry Pi general-purpose input output pin does, why current limits matter, and how to build a simple and safe LED circuit on a breadboard. I will explain how a GPIO can act as either an input or an output, how an LED must be oriented and protected with a resistor, and how to choose a resistor using Ohm’s Law. You will also learn the critical limits: the Pi uses 3.3 volt logic, its pins are not 5 volt tolerant, and individual pins can only source or sink modest current so external drivers are needed for motors or many LEDs. Throughout, I will point out common mistakes, such as leaving out the resistor or connecting 5 volt signals directly, and give practical alternatives like voltage dividers and level shifters. By the end you will be ready to place an LED and resistor on a breadboard, calculate expected current, and verify measurements with a multimeter safely. Think of this chapter as the safety-first introduction to making reliable Pi hardware projects.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will explain how each Raspberry Pi GPIO pin behaves as an input or an output, and why the board uses 3.3 volt logic. You will choose a numbering convention and follow gpiozero practices so your code refers to the pins you expect. You will design and assemble a simple LED circuit using a breadboard and a current-limiting resistor, calculate the resistor value using Ohm’s Law, and verify measurements with a multimeter. Finally, you will apply voltage and current limits to protect the Pi, identify when to use a voltage divider or level shifter, and decide when an external transistor or motor driver is required. Each objective links a practical skill to a safety habit: knowing how the pin sources and sinks current prevents damage, calculating resistor values keeps LEDs healthy, and using level shifting preserves the SoC. These skills prepare you to build indicator lights, read sensor inputs safely, and expand to higher-power devices with proper drivers. Consider how each objective reduces risk while increasing the kinds of hardware you can control.

screens.title: What GPIO Pins Are and How They Work
screens.narratorSegment: GPIO stands for general-purpose input output and describes the pins on the Raspberry Pi that connect software to hardware. Each pin can be configured by software to act as an output, where it drives a voltage, or as an input, where it reads an external voltage. When configured as an output the pin presents either a HIGH level at 3.3 volts or a LOW level at zero volts. When configured as an input the pin will read the voltage level and let your program decide what to do. This distinction matters because driving a pin and reading a pin carry different electrical responsibilities. For example, as an output the pin sources or sinks current to power small indicators like an LED through a resistor. As an input the pin expects a safe signal within the 0 to 3.3 volt range; exceeding that can damage the processor. A common misconception is to treat pins like power rails; they are not designed to supply large currents. Another misconception is assuming all pins behave identically — some pins have special functions or default pull-up or pull-down behaviors. To practice, configure a pin as output, toggle it HIGH and LOW, and observe voltage with a multimeter. Then configure it as input and apply a known high or low signal through a safe resistor to verify readings. How confident are you that you can identify a pin’s mode and measure its level safely?

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › GPIO Definition
GPIO: programmable inputs and outputs
Pins present either a HIGH at 3.3 volts or a LOW at ground; software sets mode.
Key behaviors
  • Output: drives HIGH or LOW and can source or sink small current.
  • Input: reads external voltage and requires the signal be within 0 to 3.3 volts.
  • Some pins have pull-up or pull-down defaults to avoid floating inputs.
Concrete example
Set GPIO 17 as an output, write HIGH, and measure about 3.3 volts between the pin and ground with a multimeter.
Key Takeaway

Treat pins as logic-level signals, not power rails; always check mode and limits before wiring.

Common misconceptions
  • GPIO pins supply unlimited power like a wall adapter — false.
  • All pins are interchangeable — false; some pins have reserved roles or default pulls.
Check your understanding
If a pin configured as input reads floating values, add a pull-up or pull-down resistor or enable the internal pull option.
Practice: measure pin voltage in both modes with a meter.

screens.title: LED Basics: Anode, Cathode, and Orientation
screens.narratorSegment: An LED is a diode that emits light when current flows through it in the forward direction. It only allows current to pass from its anode to its cathode. The longer lead is the anode and should connect toward the positive side of the circuit; the shorter lead is the cathode and goes toward ground. Because LEDs are diodes they have a forward voltage drop: for a typical red LED this is about one point eight volts. Current must be limited to a safe value using a resistor, otherwise the LED can draw excessive current and fail. When you wire an LED to a GPIO pin, put the resistor in series with the LED — either between the pin and the LED or between the LED and ground — the series order does not change the electrical current. A common mistake is to insert an LED backwards and observe no light; another is to omit the resistor and damage the LED or the Pi. As a hands-on check, after wiring and before powering, gently tug each leg to confirm proper breadboard seating, and visually confirm the longer leg points to the expected positive node. Try lighting the LED at a low current first, then increase brightness by lowering resistance only within safe limits. How bright do you expect the LED to be at six to ten milliamps compared to twenty milliamps?

keyIdea.text: LEDs pass current in one direction; place anode toward positive, cathode toward ground, and always use a series resistor.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › LED Basics
LED basics and orientation
An LED is a diode: current flows one way and it drops a small forward voltage.
Anode and cathode
Long leg = anode (positive), short leg = cathode (ground). Place accordingly on the breadboard.
Forward voltage
Typical red LED forward drop ~1.8 volts; this determines the resistor voltage.
Concrete example
With a GPIO at 3.3 volts and a red LED at 1.8 volts, the resistor sees 1.5 volts and limits current to protect the LED and pin.
Quick checks
  • Is the long leg toward the positive node?
  • Is a resistor present in series?
  • Are both legs seated firmly in different rows of the breadboard?
Common mistake
Placing both LED legs in the same row so they short; always use separate rows so current passes through the LED and resistor.
Analogy: the LED is a one-way valve for current — it only allows flow in its forward direction.

screens.title: Resistor Selection with Ohm's Law
screens.narratorSegment: Resistor selection for an LED is a straightforward application of Ohm’s Law. First identify the supply voltage, which for the Raspberry Pi GPIO is three point three volts. Next find the LED forward voltage; for a typical red LED it's about one point eight volts. Subtract the LED forward voltage from the supply to find the voltage across the resistor. Then decide the desired current; a safe, bright indicator current is around six to ten milliamps. Use Ohm's Law, resistance equals voltage divided by current, to compute R. For example, with three point three volts minus one point eight volts equals one point five volts across the resistor. Dividing by zero point zero one amps yields one hundred fifty ohms. A standard two hundred twenty ohm resistor yields about six point eight milliamps, which is bright enough and safer for the Pi. Common mistakes include calculating with the wrong supply voltage or trying to run LEDs at high currents that exceed the per-pin limit. When in doubt, choose a larger resistance for safety. Practice: calculate resistor values for different LED forward voltages and currents and compare to standard resistor values available in your kit.

keyIdea.title: Ohm's Law
keyIdea.text: R = V across resistor divided by desired current; use the supply minus LED forward voltage as V.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › Resistor Selection
Resistor selection using Ohm's Law
A step-by-step process to compute a safe series resistor for an LED.
Steps
  1. Identify supply voltage: 3.3 volts for GPIO.
  2. Find LED forward voltage, for red ~1.8 volts.
  3. Compute resistor voltage: supply minus LED drop.
  4. Choose desired current, e.g., 10 mA.
  5. Compute R = V divided by I and pick the nearest higher standard resistor.
Worked example
3.3 minus 1.8 is 1.5 volts. At 10 milliamps, R = 1.5 divided by 0.01 equals 150 ohms. Use 220 ohms for a safer current of 6.8 milliamps.
Tip
If unsure, pick a larger resistor to reduce current and protect the GPIO pin and LED.
Key Takeaway

Use the supply minus LED forward voltage as the resistor voltage, then divide by desired current to find R.

screens.title: Wiring the LED and Resistor on a Breadboard
screens.narratorSegment: Assembling the LED and resistor on a breadboard is a practical skill that benefits from a checklist. Begin by powering down the Raspberry Pi to avoid accidental shorts. Identify the GPIO pin you will use, and confirm whether you refer to it by BOARD or BCM numbering. Place the LED so that its legs occupy separate rows; the anode goes toward the pin row and the cathode toward ground. Insert the resistor in series with the LED so that current must pass through both components. Use a jumper wire to connect the GPIO pin to the row containing the anode or resistor, and another jumper from the cathode row to a ground pin on the Pi. Before powering, visually inspect that you did not connect a 5 volt pin to a GPIO pin and that no wires cross unexpectedly. After powering, measure the voltage at the GPIO when the pin is HIGH; you should see roughly three point three volts, and the resistor should show the expected voltage drop. If the LED is dimmer than expected, re-check resistor value and seating of components. This methodical approach reduces mistakes and protects the board and components.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › Breadboard Wiring
Wiring the LED and resistor
A safe, repeatable assembly flow for your breadboard session.
Step-by-step
  1. Power off the Pi.
  2. Confirm numbering: BOARD or BCM and locate chosen pin.
  3. Place LED with legs in separate rows; long leg toward GPIO.
  4. Place resistor in series with LED in the same current path.
  5. Connect jumper from GPIO to LED/resistor row and jumper from cathode to ground.
  6. Inspect wiring and then power on to test.
Verification
  • Measure GPIO voltage when HIGH; expect about 3.3 volts.
  • Measure voltage across resistor to compute actual current.
  • If values differ, power down and re-check connections and resistor value.
Key Takeaway

Follow the checklist and verify voltages before and after powering to avoid damage.

screens.title: 3.3V Logic vs 5V Logic: Level Shifting Options
screens.narratorSegment: Raspberry Pi GPIO uses three point three volt logic and is not tolerant of five volt signals. That means you must never connect a five volt output directly to a GPIO input; doing so risks permanent damage to the SoC. To interface with five volt devices you have two common safe options: a passive voltage divider or a dedicated logic level shifter. A voltage divider uses two resistors to reduce a higher voltage to a lower voltage and can work for simple, low-speed signals. However, voltage dividers can be sensitive to input impedance and are less reliable for bidirectional or high-speed signals. A dedicated level shifter, often implemented with MOSFETs or specialized ICs, provides proper direction handling, buffering, and predictable thresholds and is the safer choice for many projects. Another safe approach is to use sensors and modules that already operate at three point three volts or to power external modules separately while using a proper translator between logic levels. A common misconception is assuming a single resistor to ground will protect a GPIO; it will not safely translate logic levels. Evaluate signal direction, speed, and reliability needs when picking a method.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › 3.3V vs 5V
3.3 volt logic and interfacing options
Understand the trade-offs between voltage dividers and level shifters.
Voltage divider
Two resistors reduce voltage for simple, unidirectional signals. Watch out for input impedance and speed limits.
Level shifter
Designed for reliable bidirectional communication and predictable thresholds; safer for many use cases.
When to use divider
Simple sensor outputs at low speed and one direction only.
When to use shifter
Bidirectional buses, higher speed communications, or unknown input impedance.
Quick safety rule
If unsure, pick a level shifter or choose a three point three volt device to avoid risk.

screens.title: GPIO Current Limits and When to Use Drivers
screens.narratorSegment: Each Raspberry Pi GPIO pin can source or sink a limited amount of current, typically up to around sixteen milliamps per pin. Equally important is the board-wide limit: the total current drawn across GPIO pins should remain below roughly fifty milliamps. These limits are much lower than typical Arduino pin capabilities and are why high-current devices cannot be driven directly. When an LED or small sensor is within those limits, you can power it directly through a series resistor. When a device requires more current, such as motors, solenoids, or large LED arrays, route its power through an external transistor or a dedicated motor driver. An NPN transistor can act as a switch: a small current from the GPIO controls the transistor, which switches a higher current from an external supply to the load. Motor driver modules like the L298N or L293D provide directional control and protect against back-emf. A common misconception is to think the GPIO pin must provide the motor voltage; instead, the GPIO provides a control signal while the motor draws current from its own supply controlled by the transistor or driver. Always plan for separate power and proper common grounds when using external supplies.

keyIdea.title: Current limits
keyIdea.text: Pins ~16 mA each, total below ~50 mA; use transistors or motor drivers and external supplies for higher current needs.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › Current Limits
GPIO current limits and external drivers
Understand when a transistor or driver is required to protect the Pi.
Per-pin and total limits
Pins can source or sink around 16 mA each; keep total GPIO current below about 50 mA.
When to use drivers
Use drivers or transistors for motors, many LEDs, or any load that needs more current than a pin can safely provide.
NPN transistor
A small GPIO current controls a larger current from an external supply to the load.
Motor driver module
Provides direction control and protects against back-emf from motors.
Practical rule
If the device draws more than the per-pin safe current, use an external driver and separate power source with a common ground.

screens.title: Using an NPN Transistor to Switch Higher Currents
screens.narratorSegment: When a load needs more current than a GPIO can provide, an NPN transistor can act as a low-side switch controlled by the GPIO. The GPIO provides a small base current through a base resistor to the transistor, which allows a larger collector current from an external power source to flow through the load to ground. The load receives power from the external supply, not directly from the GPIO. Always include a base resistor to limit current into the transistor's base and protect the GPIO. Also include a flyback diode across inductive loads like motors to protect against voltage spikes when the device switches off. A common wiring arrangement places the transistor between the load and ground, the load between the positive external supply and the transistor collector, and the emitter to ground. Be sure to share a common ground between the Pi and the external supply so the transistor base reference is correct. A frequent misconception is to wire the transistor without a base resistor or without a common ground — both can cause unpredictable behavior or component damage. Practice wiring a small lamp or fan via a transistor with an external supply and verify that the GPIO only sources a few milliamps while the load draws its required current from the external source.

keyIdea.title: Transistor switch
keyIdea.text: Use an NPN transistor with a base resistor and a shared ground to switch higher currents from an external supply while keeping GPIO current low.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › Transistor Switching
Switching higher currents with an NPN transistor
Let the transistor carry the heavy current; the GPIO only provides the control current.
Wiring pattern
  • Emitter to ground.
  • Collector to load; load to external positive supply.
  • GPIO to base through a base resistor.
  • Share common ground between Pi and external supply.
Protection
Add a flyback diode across inductive loads and a base resistor to limit GPIO current into the transistor base.
Key Takeaway

Transistors let your GPIO control larger currents safely; always include proper resistors, diodes, and a common ground.

screens.title: gpiozero Conventions and Pin Numbering Choices
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right pin numbering convention and following gpiozero conventions helps avoid wiring mistakes. There are two common numbering schemes: BOARD and BCM. BOARD refers to the physical pin positions on the header, whereas BCM refers to the Broadcom chip numbering for each GPIO signal. Pick one scheme and use it consistently in wiring and code. The gpiozero library follows a simple device-oriented approach; for example you create an LED object tied to a pin and call methods to turn it on or off. This pattern reduces direct pin management and makes scripts easier to read. A common source of errors is mixing BOARD and BCM references between the wiring diagram and the code, which causes unexpected pins to be driven. screens.title: Safe Wiring Practices and Powering Up
screens.narratorSegment: Safe wiring begins before you touch power. Always power down the Raspberry Pi before connecting or disconnecting jumper wires to the GPIO header. Double-check that you are not connecting a five volt power pin to a GPIO; a momentary short between 5V and a GPIO pin can instantly damage the board. Keep jumper wires organized, avoid loose stray wires that can bridge pins, and use a breadboard with clear spacing so components do not accidentally short. When making changes, follow a step-by-step routine: power down, make the wiring change, inspect visually, then power up. Use insulating sleeves or shrouded connectors for exposed 5V and ground lines when possible. When testing, measure voltages with a multimeter first at low expectation points before connecting sensitive inputs. A common mistake is hot-plugging devices or swapping ground and power mistakenly; these simple errors cause the majority of hardware failures. Finally, keep a list of pin assignments and a quick diagram near the workspace so you and others follow the same wiring plan. screens.title: Hands-on: Build and Measure an LED Circuit on GPIO 17
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity guides you through building the LED circuit on GPIO seventeen and verifying the expected current with a multimeter. First, power down the Pi and note whether you will use BCM numbering; locate GPIO seventeen. Place the LED and a two hundred twenty ohm resistor in series between GPIO seventeen and ground on the breadboard. Using our earlier calculation for a red LED with a one point eight volt drop, the resistor sees about one point five volts so a two hundred twenty ohm resistor produces roughly six point eight milliamps. Power the Pi and set GPIO seventeen HIGH; measure the voltage across the resistor with your multimeter, then compute current by dividing measured resistor voltage by two hundred twenty ohms. Compare the measured current to the calculated value and note small differences due to LED forward voltage tolerances or meter accuracy. If the current is significantly higher than expected, power down immediately and re-check wiring and resistor value. This practical measurement connects calculation to reality and reinforces safe habits. What did your measurements reveal about component tolerances in your kit?

Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › Hands-on Activity
Build and measure: LED on GPIO 17
A guided lab: assemble the circuit, calculate current, and verify with a multimeter.
Step checklist
  1. Power off and locate GPIO 17 using BCM numbering.
  2. Place LED and 220 ohm resistor in series between GPIO 17 and ground.
  3. Power on and set GPIO 17 HIGH.
  4. Measure voltage across resistor; I equals V divided by R.
  5. Compare measured current with calculated expected current.
Expected calculation
With 3.3 V supply and 1.8 V LED drop, resistor sees 1.5 V. At 220 ohms, expected current ≈ 6.8 mA.

Second, always use a current-limiting resistor with LEDs and calculate its value using Ohm's Law, using supply minus LED forward voltage as the resistor voltage. These three points capture the most important safety and design concerns you will apply in projects. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn what each Raspberry Pi general-purpose input output pin does, why current limits matter, and how to build a simple and safe LED circuit on a breadboard. I will explain how a GPIO can act as either an input or an output, how an LED must be oriented and protected with a resistor, and how to choose a resistor using Ohm’s Law. You will also learn the critical limits: the Pi uses 3.3 volt logic, its pins are not 5 volt tolerant, and individual pins can only source or sink modest current so external drivers are needed for motors or many LEDs. Throughout, I will point out common mistakes, such as leaving out the resistor or connecting 5 volt signals directly, and give practical alternatives like voltage dividers and level shifters. By the end you will be ready to place an LED and resistor on a breadboard, calculate expected current, and verify measurements with a multimeter safely. Think of this chapter as the safety-first introduction to making reliable Pi hardware projects.

By the end of this chapter you will explain how each Raspberry Pi GPIO pin behaves as an input or an output, and why the board uses 3.3 volt logic. You will choose a numbering convention and follow gpiozero practices so your code refers to the pins you expect. You will design and assemble a simple LED circuit using a breadboard and a current-limiting resistor, calculate the resistor value using Ohm’s Law, and verify measurements with a multimeter. Finally, you will apply voltage and current limits to protect the Pi, identify when to use a voltage divider or level shifter, and decide when an external transistor or motor driver is required. Each objective links a practical skill to a safety habit: knowing how the pin sources and sinks current prevents damage, calculating resistor values keeps LEDs healthy, and using level shifting preserves the SoC. These skills prepare you to build indicator lights, read sensor inputs safely, and expand to higher-power devices with proper drivers. Consider how each objective reduces risk while increasing the kinds of hardware you can control.

This screen focuses on lab-ready objectives. You will correctly orient an LED by identifying anode and cathode, recognize resistor color bands to choose an approximate value, and mount the components in series on a breadboard. You will also practice safe power procedures: always power down before wiring, double-check pin numbers against your numbering convention, and confirm you have a current-limiting resistor in place before applying voltage. You will learn to use a multimeter to measure voltage across the resistor and compute the actual current, then compare that measured current to your Ohm’s Law calculation. Finally, you will develop a simple decision flow: if a device draws more than the per-pin safe current, route it through a transistor or driver and power it from an external supply. These lab objectives convert conceptual rules into repeatable actions you can follow when building projects. Keep focusing on safety first, then correctness. How will you double-check your wiring before you switch the Pi on?

GPIO stands for general-purpose input output and describes the pins on the Raspberry Pi that connect software to hardware. Each pin can be configured by software to act as an output, where it drives a voltage, or as an input, where it reads an external voltage. When configured as an output the pin presents either a HIGH level at 3.3 volts or a LOW level at zero volts. When configured as an input the pin will read the voltage level and let your program decide what to do. This distinction matters because driving a pin and reading a pin carry different electrical responsibilities. For example, as an output the pin sources or sinks current to power small indicators like an LED through a resistor. As an input the pin expects a safe signal within the 0 to 3.3 volt range; exceeding that can damage the processor. A common misconception is to treat pins like power rails; they are not designed to supply large currents. Another misconception is assuming all pins behave identically — some pins have special functions or default pull-up or pull-down behaviors. To practice, configure a pin as output, toggle it HIGH and LOW, and observe voltage with a multimeter. Then configure it as input and apply a known high or low signal through a safe resistor to verify readings. How confident are you that you can identify a pin’s mode and measure its level safely?

An LED is a diode that emits light when current flows through it in the forward direction. It only allows current to pass from its anode to its cathode. The longer lead is the anode and should connect toward the positive side of the circuit; the shorter lead is the cathode and goes toward ground. Because LEDs are diodes they have a forward voltage drop: for a typical red LED this is about one point eight volts. Current must be limited to a safe value using a resistor, otherwise the LED can draw excessive current and fail. When you wire an LED to a GPIO pin, put the resistor in series with the LED — either between the pin and the LED or between the LED and ground — the series order does not change the electrical current. A common mistake is to insert an LED backwards and observe no light; another is to omit the resistor and damage the LED or the Pi. As a hands-on check, after wiring and before powering, gently tug each leg to confirm proper breadboard seating, and visually confirm the longer leg points to the expected positive node. Try lighting the LED at a low current first, then increase brightness by lowering resistance only within safe limits. How bright do you expect the LED to be at six to ten milliamps compared to twenty milliamps?

Resistor selection for an LED is a straightforward application of Ohm’s Law. First identify the supply voltage, which for the Raspberry Pi GPIO is three point three volts. Next find the LED forward voltage; for a typical red LED it's about one point eight volts. Subtract the LED forward voltage from the supply to find the voltage across the resistor. Then decide the desired current; a safe, bright indicator current is around six to ten milliamps. Use Ohm's Law, resistance equals voltage divided by current, to compute R. For example, with three point three volts minus one point eight volts equals one point five volts across the resistor. Dividing by zero point zero one amps yields one hundred fifty ohms. A standard two hundred twenty ohm resistor yields about six point eight milliamps, which is bright enough and safer for the Pi. Common mistakes include calculating with the wrong supply voltage or trying to run LEDs at high currents that exceed the per-pin limit. When in doubt, choose a larger resistance for safety. Practice: calculate resistor values for different LED forward voltages and currents and compare to standard resistor values available in your kit.

Assembling the LED and resistor on a breadboard is a practical skill that benefits from a checklist. Begin by powering down the Raspberry Pi to avoid accidental shorts. Identify the GPIO pin you will use, and confirm whether you refer to it by BOARD or BCM numbering. Place the LED so that its legs occupy separate rows; the anode goes toward the pin row and the cathode toward ground. Insert the resistor in series with the LED so that current must pass through both components. Use a jumper wire to connect the GPIO pin to the row containing the anode or resistor, and another jumper from the cathode row to a ground pin on the Pi. Before powering, visually inspect that you did not connect a 5 volt pin to a GPIO pin and that no wires cross unexpectedly. After powering, measure the voltage at the GPIO when the pin is HIGH; you should see roughly three point three volts, and the resistor should show the expected voltage drop. If the LED is dimmer than expected, re-check resistor value and seating of components. This methodical approach reduces mistakes and protects the board and components.

Raspberry Pi GPIO uses three point three volt logic and is not tolerant of five volt signals. That means you must never connect a five volt output directly to a GPIO input; doing so risks permanent damage to the SoC. To interface with five volt devices you have two common safe options: a passive voltage divider or a dedicated logic level shifter. A voltage divider uses two resistors to reduce a higher voltage to a lower voltage and can work for simple, low-speed signals. However, voltage dividers can be sensitive to input impedance and are less reliable for bidirectional or high-speed signals. A dedicated level shifter, often implemented with MOSFETs or specialized ICs, provides proper direction handling, buffering, and predictable thresholds and is the safer choice for many projects. Another safe approach is to use sensors and modules that already operate at three point three volts or to power external modules separately while using a proper translator between logic levels. A common misconception is assuming a single resistor to ground will protect a GPIO; it will not safely translate logic levels. Evaluate signal direction, speed, and reliability needs when picking a method.

Each Raspberry Pi GPIO pin can source or sink a limited amount of current, typically up to around sixteen milliamps per pin. Equally important is the board-wide limit: the total current drawn across GPIO pins should remain below roughly fifty milliamps. These limits are much lower than typical Arduino pin capabilities and are why high-current devices cannot be driven directly. When an LED or small sensor is within those limits, you can power it directly through a series resistor. When a device requires more current, such as motors, solenoids, or large LED arrays, route its power through an external transistor or a dedicated motor driver. An NPN transistor can act as a switch: a small current from the GPIO controls the transistor, which switches a higher current from an external supply to the load. Motor driver modules like the L298N or L293D provide directional control and protect against back-emf. A common misconception is to think the GPIO pin must provide the motor voltage; instead, the GPIO provides a control signal while the motor draws current from its own supply controlled by the transistor or driver. Always plan for separate power and proper common grounds when using external supplies.

When a load needs more current than a GPIO can provide, an NPN transistor can act as a low-side switch controlled by the GPIO. The GPIO provides a small base current through a base resistor to the transistor, which allows a larger collector current from an external power source to flow through the load to ground. The load receives power from the external supply, not directly from the GPIO. Always include a base resistor to limit current into the transistor's base and protect the GPIO. Also include a flyback diode across inductive loads like motors to protect against voltage spikes when the device switches off. A common wiring arrangement places the transistor between the load and ground, the load between the positive external supply and the transistor collector, and the emitter to ground. Be sure to share a common ground between the Pi and the external supply so the transistor base reference is correct. A frequent misconception is to wire the transistor without a base resistor or without a common ground — both can cause unpredictable behavior or component damage. Practice wiring a small lamp or fan via a transistor with an external supply and verify that the GPIO only sources a few milliamps while the load draws its required current from the external source.
